title: One Missing Protein, A Cortex Built Wrong

scenes.visual: Show the existing title over a normal cortex beside a disorganized reeler cortex. Introduce no extra biological claims.

scenes.tts: Reelin is needed for neurons to take their proper places in the developing brain. A mouse without this protein reels as it walks. Its cerebellum is small, and its cortical layers are disorganized and roughly reversed. The problem is placement: neurons are made on schedule, but settle in the wrong order.

scenes.visual: Name Reelin immediately. Show a wobbling reeler mouse, its small cerebellum and a normal cortex beside a disorganized, roughly inverted cortex. Mark Reelin as missing in reeler. Show matching birth schedules but different final neuronal positions; make placement the central contrast.

scenes.tts: Normally, neurons climb from the ventricular zone toward the surface. The first ones form a thin sheet, the preplate. The next wave enters that sheet and splits it. Each new wave then climbs past the last. Early-born neurons end up deep. Late-born neurons end up near the surface.

scenes.visual: Keep the normal cortex slab and birth-order colors. Animate preplate formation and splitting, then successive waves passing earlier neurons. Label early-born deep and late-born superficial. Reserve the source of Reelin for s05_source.

scenes.tts: Birthdating showed the same classes of neurons, born on the same schedule, in reeler mice. But the preplate fails to split. Later waves tend to stop beneath the neurons already there. Early-born neurons tend to sit near the surface, and late-born neurons deep. Reelin is needed for normal layering.

scenes.visual: Compare normal and reeler slabs with matching birthdate colors and schedules. In reeler, leave the preplate unsplit and show later waves tending to accumulate beneath earlier neurons. Preserve visible disorganization as well as approximate inversion; do not depict a perfectly reversed stack.

scenes.tts: How does the signal get inside a neuron? Reelin binds two lipoprotein receptors, Apo E R two and V L D L R. Inside, the kinases Fyn and Sark add phosphate to the adaptor Dab one. Phosphorylated Dab one recruits effectors. Cullin five then helps mark it for destruction, limiting the signal.
scenes.narration: How does the signal get inside a neuron? Reelin binds two lipoprotein receptors, ApoER2 and VLDLR. Inside, the kinases Fyn and Src add phosphate to the adaptor Dab1. Phosphorylated Dab1 recruits effectors. Cullin 5 then helps mark it for destruction, limiting the signal.

scenes.visual: Start with extracellular Reelin binding teal ApoER2 and VLDLR on the neuronal membrane. Show pink Fyn and Src adding a gold phosphate to purple Dab1, then downstream effector recruitment. Add the off switch: Cullin 5-dependent ubiquitin marking and degradation of phosphorylated Dab1. Do not introduce the source cells until s05_source.

scenes.tts: Remove a runner from a relay and the baton never arrives. Mice without Reelin, without Dab one, or without both receptors have matching defects. That suggests one pathway. Biochemistry gives the order: brains without Reelin have more Dab one, but less phosphorylated Dab one.

scenes.tts: Where does Reelin come from? In the developing cortex, Cajal-Retzius cells secrete it in the marginal zone, at the surface. That puts the signal near the place where each new wave of neurons should settle.

scenes.visual: Return to the normal cortex slab. Highlight yellow Cajal-Retzius cells in the marginal zone releasing yellow Reelin. Mark the marginal zone above the cortical plate and show neurons settling just beneath it. Do not use a stop sign or imply a required concentration gradient.

scenes.tts: On one view, Reelin acts at specific steps of migration. Signaling through Dab one and Rap one has been linked to orienting multipolar neurons and to adhesion through N-cadherin. In the final step, somal translocation, a neuron anchors its leading process in the marginal zone and pulls its cell body up, without glial support. The effect depends on the stage: orientation, adhesion, and that final movement help neurons take their places.
